## What this area covers

{{< include _scope.md >}}

## What is known

- **Caregivers already use general chatbots, mostly to look things up.** In a national US panel of
  1,300 caregivers, a quarter of those who used chatbots had used one for caregiving, most often for
  information and less often for emotional support ([Understanding America Study](#entry-monin2026prevalence)).
  Among 272 caregivers on an advocacy group's email list, 59% had tried AI for caregiving, most often
  to make sense of a diagnosis ([Caregiver Action Network](#entry-caregiver2026shaping)). Microsoft's
  researchers report that about one in seven health conversations with Copilot concerned someone else
  ([Copilot](#entry-costagomes2026people)).
- **Caregivers ask for the same things across countries and conditions.** In interviews and focus
  groups they value answers at any hour in plain words. They worry about accuracy, privacy and losing
  human contact, and they want AI to add to human help and to hand them to a person when a situation
  is serious.
- **Experts rate general chatbots' answers to caregivers' questions as mostly accurate, with
  recurring faults.** Across dementia, stroke, mild cognitive impairment, late-life depression and
  end-of-life care, answers ran long, read at a college level, seldom cited sources and sometimes
  left out key steps. In one study they named local services that do not exist
  ([stroke rehabilitation](#entry-neo2024use)). Crisis is the weakest point: models caught about 12% to
  45% of crisis signs in scripted caregiver conversations ([InvisibleBench](#entry-madad2025invisiblebench)),
  and gave clinically acceptable answers to 37% to 63% of high-risk questions about late-life
  depression ([late-life depression](#entry-xiao2026large)).
- **Who asks changes the answer.** Models give a caregiver less concrete guidance and more advice to
  see a professional than a clinician asking the same question ([CoRUS](#entry-kaur2026who),
  [Curbside Chatbots](#entry-flathers2026curbside)), and they often give way when a caregiver pushes
  for a less suitable option ([CareDistance](#entry-mishra2026pleasing)).
- **Tools built for caregivers do better on accuracy and sources, and one trial shows a modest
  benefit.** Grounding a model in curated caregiving material improved its accuracy and its citations
  ([CaLM](#entry-parmanto2024reliable)). In the one full randomized trial here, 274 dementia caregivers
  in 43 countries who used PDC30, an online program built around an AI counselling chatbot, had less
  depression and burden after one month than those still waiting for it ([PDC30](#entry-cheng2026intervention)).

## What is missing

Read from this area's entries, which come from the searches described below:

- **Trials that measure what happens to caregivers.** Beyond the PDC30 trial, the studies here are
  pilots, protocols, comparisons without random assignment and tests of model answers. None follows
  caregivers using a general chatbot as they already do, to see whether it helps or harms them or the
  person they care for.
- **Caregivers as judges.** Most evaluations score answers to questions researchers wrote or
  caregivers posted, rated by clinicians or by another model. Caregivers rated the answers in few of
  them, as [a scoping review](#entry-gallagher2026scoping) also found.
- **Conditions beyond dementia, and medicines.** Dementia dominates. Few entries test how AI answers a
  caregiver's question about another adult's medicines, or questions of consent and whose wishes
  count.
- **Conversations over time.** Nearly every evaluation is a single question or a short scripted
  chat. How answers change over months of use is untested here; it is the subject of the theme
  [AI over a long relationship](../#theme-ai-over-a-long-relationship).
- **Who is studied.** Most samples are small and come from the US, China and Europe. Caregivers from
  minority, rural and non-English-speaking communities appear in a handful of design studies
  ([Lola](#entry-bosco2025designing), [PflegeBot](#entry-gencer2026co),
  [cultural prompting](#entry-xie2025cultural)).
